title: Phases of Retirement: Three Stages and Money Decisions
metaDescription: What are the phases of retirement? Compare the go-go, slow-go, and no-go stages, fixed IRS milestones, and how inflation shifts spending across each phase.
h1: Phases of Retirement and the Decisions in Each Stage
cardBlurb: A practical walk through the three common stages of retirement, the fixed tax milestones that govern withdrawals, and how inflation shifts spending over time.
introText:
There is no single official list for the phases of retirement. Financial planners commonly divide retirement into early, middle, and late stages, frequently using the informal labels go-go, slow-go, and no-go. Each phase brings distinct financial tasks. Early retirement centers on income timing and distribution rules. Middle retirement requires managing required minimum distributions and taxes. Late retirement deals with managing accounts, and the compounding effect of inflation on fixed living expenses.

 The [Internal Revenue Service (IRS)](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-required-minimum-distributions-rmds) does not use retirement phases, and its calendar rules do not follow lifestyle stages. Its rules set hard guardrails on taxes and penalties, while health, family circumstances, and personal spending dictate when you move from an active lifestyle to a quieter one.

sections.heading: The Phases of Retirement and the Money Decisions in Each
sections.body:
Retirement planning shorthand groups life after work into three primary phases based on physical activity and lifestyle goals. In search queries observed on Google Autocomplete, people also ask about four phases or six phases, as well as general stages of retirement. Because no statutory definition exists, whether you use three, four, or six buckets matters less than organizing the decisions that belong to each phase. Phase boundaries depend on your health, energy, and personal plans. They do not depend on a birthday.

| Phase | What Usually Changes | Money Decisions to Settle |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Early (Go-Go) | Described as the most active years, right after leaving full-time work | Account withdrawal sequence, pension options, the 401(k) rollover choice, bridge health coverage |
| Middle (Slow-Go) | Described as a slower pace | Required minimum distributions (RMDs), taxable income management, portfolio risk adjustments |
| Late (No-Go) | Described as the least active years | Who can act on your accounts, beneficiary reviews, how care would be paid for |

The early retirement phase centers on initial withdrawals and account order. You must decide which accounts to tap first. You also must determine how to bridge health insurance if you step away from work before qualifying for government healthcare programs.

During the middle stage, statutory tax obligations begin. The federal government requires you to withdraw minimum balances from traditional accounts. Late retirement shifts the focus toward managing routine daily living costs, addressing care support needs, and ensuring trusted individuals have legal authority to assist with financial management.

sections.heading: The Dates That Are Fixed by Rule
sections.body:
While lifestyle phases remain flexible, statutory deadlines set by the IRS are rigid. Missing these calendar milestones can trigger tax penalties.

| Age or Event | Applicable Accounts | Federal Rule or Requirement |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Age 55 (Separation from service) | Qualified plans only, such as 401(k) plans (not IRAs) | No 10% penalty on withdrawals from the plan of the employer you left during or after the year you turn 55 (age 50 for qualifying public safety employees in governmental plans) |
| Age 59½ | IRAs, 401(k) plans, 403(b) plans, and other qualified retirement plans | General exception to the 10% additional tax on early distributions |
| Age 73 or 75 | Traditional IRAs, SEP IRAs, SIMPLE IRAs, and employer retirement plans | Required minimum distributions must begin; start age depends on birth year per federal statutory updates |
| April 1 after first RMD year | Traditional IRAs and qualified employer plans | Final deadline for taking your very first RMD, though delaying requires taking two distributions in year two |
| Still working at sponsoring employer | Current employer retirement plan (does not apply to IRAs) | Option to delay RMDs from your current employer plan until the year you actually retire, provided you do not own 5% or more of the employer |
| Any age during owner's life | Roth IRAs and designated Roth 401(k) or Roth 403(b) accounts | No required minimum distributions during the account owner's lifetime |
| Missed distribution deadline | Traditional IRAs and employer plans subject to RMDs | 25% excise tax on the amount not distributed, reducible to 10% if corrected within two years |

Under federal tax law, money taken from an individual retirement account (IRA) or qualified retirement plan before age 59½ is considered an early distribution. Early distributions carry an additional 10% penalty tax unless a specific statutory exception applies. One prominent exception is the rule of 55. If you separate from service with an employer during or after the calendar year in which you reach age 55, distributions from that specific employer's qualified plan avoid the 10% penalty. This rule applies to employer plans like a 401(k), but it does not apply to traditional IRAs, SEP IRAs, SIMPLE IRAs, or SARSEPs. For qualifying public safety employees under governmental plans, that threshold drops to age 50. To compare this structure against scheduled equal periodic payments, review our breakdown of the [rule of 55 vs 72(t)](/compare/rule-of-55-vs-72t/).

Once you reach your designated distribution age, the IRS requires you to begin annual withdrawals from pre-tax accounts. The base starting age is 73 on current IRS topic pages. As outlined in our guide on [how to withdraw from a 401(k)](/guides/how-to-withdraw-from-401k/), federal statutory changes under the [SECURE 2.0 Act](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/retirement-plan-and-ira-required-minimum-distributions-faqs) set the RMD age at 73 for workers born between 1951 and 1959, and increase the age to 75 for individuals born in 1960 or later. Confirm your exact start date for your birth year using our [RMD calculator](/retirement/rmd-calculator/). If you fail to withdraw the required amount on time, the IRS imposes a 25% excise tax on the undistributed balance, which drops to 10% if corrected within a two-year recovery window.

sections.heading: What Inflation Does to the Same Lifestyle Across the Phases
sections.body:
A lifestyle that feels easily affordable in the early phase can strain your finances decades later because inflation continuously erodes purchasing power. In our internal modeling, we grew $60,000 of today's annual spending at 2%, 3%, and 4% a year to see what that exact same lifestyle costs at ages 75 and 85. The calculation applies the compound growth formula: $60,000 multiplied by (1 + annual rate) raised to the number of years. This calculation represents pure arithmetic. It is not an economic forecast. Real spending can rise or fall over time for personal reasons that flat arithmetic ignores, and annual inflation rates fluctuate from year to year.

| Annual Inflation Rate | Annual Cost at Age 65 | Annual Cost at Age 75 (10 Years) | Annual Cost at Age 85 (20 Years) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 2% Inflation | $60,000 | $73,140 | $89,157 |
| 3% Inflation | $60,000 | $80,635 | $108,367 |
| 4% Inflation | $60,000 | $88,815 | $131,467 |

At a modest 2% annual inflation rate, buying the goods and services that cost $60,000 at age 65 demands $73,140 by age 75. By age 85, you need $89,157 each year to maintain the identical living standard. At a 3% inflation rate, the same basket of goods costs $80,635 at age 75 and jumps to $108,367 by age 85. If annual inflation runs at 4%, annual spending hits $88,815 after ten years and more than doubles to $131,467 after twenty years.

This compounding effect explains why managing portfolio withdrawals across multiple phases requires forward planning. To examine how your current balances hold up under different spending draws, test your planned numbers in our [withdrawal calculator](/investing/withdrawal-calculator/).

sections.heading: Early Retirement: What to Settle First
sections.body:
The first phase requires establishing a reliable monthly income stream and organizing your accounts. When leaving full-time work, address these initial decisions in order:

- Identify all guaranteed income sources and map out their payment start dates.
- Determine the order in which you draw down taxable brokerage accounts, traditional pre-tax accounts, and Roth balances by reviewing [retirement withdrawal strategies](/guides/retirement-withdrawal-strategies/).
- Secure bridge health insurance if you retire prior to qualifying for public healthcare programs.
- Evaluate the choices for your existing employer retirement plan, including leaving the funds in place, transferring to an IRA, or executing a distribution by reading our guide on [what to do with a 401(k) when you retire](/guides/what-to-do-with-401k-when-you-retire/).

Compare the financial tradeoffs of starting payments earlier or waiting until later using our guide on [Social Security at 62 vs 70](/compare/social-security-at-62-vs-70/). If you are evaluating overall financial readiness, use our checklist on [am I ready to retire](/guides/am-i-ready-to-retire/) to review your baseline.

sections.heading: Middle and Late Retirement: What Changes
sections.body:
Moving into the middle stage of retirement shifts your primary financial task from initiating income to managing mandatory taxes. Required minimum distributions start at 73, or 75 if you were born in 1960 or later. 

In the late phase, daily life changes again. Because care costs can be unpredictable, your late-stage plan should address who will manage your accounts if you experience health challenges. 

Securing dependable income that does not depend on active portfolio management helps anchor late-stage budgets. When reviewing guaranteed cash flow, evaluate the core differences between a pension and an annuity in our analysis of a [pension vs annuity](/compare/pension-vs-annuity/). Retirees can also review the rules for a [qualified longevity annuity contract (QLAC)](/guides/qlac-qualified-longevity-annuity-contract/). If you want to evaluate how timing your retirement affects physical well-being, explore our guide on the [ideal retirement age for your health](/guides/ideal-retirement-age-for-your-health/).

sections.heading: Who This Framework Does Not Fit
sections.body:
The standard three-phase model assumes a gradual, voluntary transition from an active career into full leisure. This structure does not fit everyone.

A sudden health event alters the entire timeline. If chronic illness or acute disability forces an unplanned early departure from the workforce, active travel plans may vanish entirely. Similarly, couples where spouses have significant age differences or divergent career timelines will find that one partner enters a slower phase while the other remains active in the workforce.

Retirees who continue working part-time, consult, or operate small businesses also break the traditional mold. 





If you want professional help mapping your personalized spending needs, read our assessment on whether a [financial advisor is worth it](/guides/financial-advisor-worth-it/) to help evaluate professional fee structures.

sections.heading: Our Takeaway
sections.body:
Treat the phases as a way to order your decisions. They are not a calendar schedule. Settle your core income streams, account withdrawal sequences, and 401(k) rollover choices during the early stage. Prepare your portfolio for mandatory distributions and taxable income shifts in the middle years. Account for compounding price increases in the late stage. Based on our internal modeling, maintaining a $60,000 lifestyle today requires $80,635 at age 75 and $108,367 at age 85 at a 3% inflation rate.

This framework fits individuals who are within a few years of stepping away from work, or who recently retired, and want an organized approach to sequencing major financial decisions. It does not fit a worker forced into early retirement by unexpected illness or an involuntary job loss, where survival cash flow supersedes long-term phase modeling. Your personal trajectory will shift based on your physical health, whether you receive guaranteed pension or annuity income, and how your household's actual annual living costs evolve. Calculate your projected lifetime retirement cash flow with our free [retirement income calculator](/retirement/retirement-income-calculator/) to set your target numbers.

faqs.question: What are the three phases of retirement?
faqs.answer: The three phases of retirement are commonly described as early, middle, and late retirement. In financial planning discussions, they are frequently called the go-go, slow-go, and no-go years to reflect shifts in physical energy and activity. Planners use these labels for a more active early period, a slower middle and a least-active late period. The IRS does not use them.

faqs.question: What are the go-go, slow-go and no-go years?
faqs.answer: Go-go, slow-go, and no-go are informal labels used by retirement planners to describe changes in lifestyle activity. Planners use these labels for a more active early period, a slower middle and a least-active late period. The IRS does not use them.

faqs.question: How many phases of retirement are there?
faqs.answer: There is no single official count for the phases of retirement. In search queries observed on Google Autocomplete, people search for three phases, four phases, and six phases, as well as general stages. The IRS does not recognize formal phase counts or assign age limits to them. The phases serve purely as an informal framework to help retirees plan the timing of financial decisions.

faqs.question: At what age do required withdrawals start?
faqs.answer: Required minimum distributions from traditional pre-tax retirement accounts generally begin at age 73 according to current IRS guidance. Federal statutory rules established by the [SECURE 2.0 Act](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/retirement-plan-and-ira-required-minimum-distributions-faqs) set the RMD age at 73 for account owners born between 1951 and 1959, and increase the age to 75 for anyone born in 1960 or later. [Account owners must confirm their specific required start age](https://www.irs.gov/retirement-plans/retirement-plan-and-ira-required-minimum-distributions-faqs) based on their birth year.

faqs.question: Does spending go down in retirement?
faqs.answer: Spending patterns vary by household, and economic arithmetic shows that inflation increases the dollar cost of maintaining the same lifestyle over time. Real spending can fall or rise for reasons the arithmetic ignores. Tracking your actual household expenses provides a more reliable picture than assuming costs will drop automatically.
